title: Representing chosen numbers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)
header: Representing chosen numbers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
### Prerequisites

This game practices what we learned in the previous activity (<htcite0>), where the abacus taught, step by step, how to write a number bead by bead. Here you choose the number yourself: any value from **0.99999999** to **999999999** that fits in the nine columns of the abacus. We recommend completing that practice first.

source.page: Writing numbers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
### Representing the number you choose

Recognizing the importance of practice exercises as a way to reinforce knowledge (<htcite0>), we present below a game that uses the same abacus board as the previous practices. This time the abacus does **not** draw a random number: you type the number you want to practice.

#### How the game works

Write a number between **0.99999999** and **999999999** in the box, using a period (.) as the decimal separator. It must fit in the nine columns of the abacus, so the digits before the decimal point plus the digits after it cannot be more than nine (for example, `12345.6789`, `999999999` and `0.99999999` are valid). Keeping the pattern used with integer numbers, the decimal point (⚫) starts at the rightmost column: the column where it sits is the units.

Click **Represent** to start the challenge: move the decimal point (⚫) and activate the beads until the abacus shows your number. The "Value" readout shows what is on the board at each moment. As soon as everything matches, you receive the congratulations.

If you cannot do it alone, click **Help me?**: the game clears the board and teaches your number step by step — first moving the decimal point (when needed), then writing each digit in its column. After the last step you can choose another number or click **Next level**.

#### The eight levels

The badge still shows the eight levels of the previous games, from **x.0** to **xxxx.ddddd**. The level is now only a progress marker: at every level you may choose any number in the allowed range, with as many integer or decimal columns as you like as long as they fit in the nine abacus columns.

source.text: Costa, M., Cardoso, A. P., Lacerda, C., Lopes, A., & Gomes, C.
